events.text: In the Will of Heaven the examination hall is lit from every side, so no candidate can hide a thought. The first paper of the Examination of the Book of Fates: index the prayers of one world for one day. There are eleven million. The examiner, an old goddess called Saebyeok, mentions that the world will notice if you lose one.

choices.text: Index every one, slowly

effects.log: You finish on the last bell with a cramped hand. Saebyeok finds one prayer filed under weather that was for a lost goat. She lets it pass. You go and find the goat afterwards.

choices.text: Sort them by what they want, not who sent them

effects.log: It is faster and it shows the shape of the world: mostly rain, mostly children, mostly please. Saebyeok marks you down for method and up for sense.

events.text: The sun-gods set the Examination of the Book of Fates at noon, and their noon lasts as long as they like. A tutor offers to prepare you. Gomun was once god of a river that silted up; now he teaches so that somebody remembers him. His fee: you pray to him once a day for a year. He has no other worshippers, and he is starting to go thin at the edges.

choices.text: Pay the fee

effects.log: You pray to him every morning. He grows a little more solid each month and his lessons get sharper. By the exam he can hold a cup again, and he cries a little when he does.

choices.text: Study alone

effects.log: You study alone and it is harder. You hear later that Gomun found another pupil, who forgot him by spring.

events.text: Candidates of the Will of Heaven sit in rows of light, and the Book is read aloud by a herald made of fire. A page of the Book of Fates has gone missing from the reading room of {cth_court}, and {cth_rival} has gone very calm about the Examination.

choices.text: Report it to the proctors

effects.log: The page is found folded in a sleeve. {cth_rival} sits the exam a cycle late and remembers you for it, which in this realm is a long time.

choices.text: Say nothing and study harder

effects.log: You study until the lamps go out. Whatever is on that page, you will have to beat it honestly.

choices.text: Take it back and return it to its shelf

ok.log: The page is back on its shelf by dawn. Nobody knows but you, and {cth_rival}, who has started watching you.

fail.log: You are found in the reading room at night with a page of the Book in your hand. It takes a week to explain.

events.text: In the Will of Heaven the examination hall is lit from every side, so no candidate can hide a thought. The essay paper: two worlds pray for the same rain and there is only one storm. Give it to one. Explain yourself to the other. Three hours. The candidate beside you has begun to weep quietly into the margin.

choices.text: Give it to the hungrier world

effects.log: You write out their granary figures and give them the rain. For the other world you write a letter of apology so good that the examiners pass it around.

choices.text: Split the storm so both get a little

effects.log: Both worlds get a drizzle and neither is saved. The examiner writes "kind, and wrong" in red, and gives you a middling mark.

choices.text: Write that the question is how wars begin

effects.log: One line, and you hand it in early. The examiner underlines it twice. It is either the best answer of the year or the worst, and nobody will say which.

events.text: The sun-gods set the Examination of the Book of Fates at noon, and their noon lasts as long as they like. Beside you sits Dolsoe, who was a mortal blacksmith forty years ago and is now, somehow, a god of anvils. He has never read anything. He holds the brush like a hammer and has broken three.

choices.text: Teach him to read at night

effects.log: Every night, by a small lamp. He learns fast once he stops hitting the letters. On exam day he writes slowly, in big square strokes, and every one of them is right.

choices.text: Lend him brushes and keep to your own work

effects.log: You lend him five brushes. He breaks four. He thanks you with a horseshoe that never rusts, which is not much use to you but you keep it.

events.text: Candidates of the Will of Heaven sit in rows of light, and the Book is read aloud by a herald made of fire. Ttukbae is sitting the Examination for the nine hundredth time. He is cheerful about it. He brings a cushion and a flask and knows every proctor's children by name. He says the trick is not to want it.

choices.text: Ask him what goes wrong

effects.log: He thinks about it for a long time. "I always answer the question I wish they had asked," he says. You decide not to do that.

choices.text: Ask him why he keeps coming

effects.log: "For the company," says Ttukbae. You share his flask. It is the most pleasant afternoon you have had in years, and you do not study at all.

events.text: In the Will of Heaven the examination hall is lit from every side, so no candidate can hide a thought. The oral examination. Your examiner is Ulsan, a mountain god, and he speaks at a mountain's pace. His question has been going for eleven years. You think you know where it is heading, but he has changed direction twice.

choices.text: Wait for the end of the question

effects.log: It ends on the fourteenth year. It was not what you thought. Your answer takes an afternoon. Ulsan seems to find that very rude, and passes you anyway.

choices.text: Answer early, where you think it is going

ok.log: You guess right. Ulsan stops, rumbles, and gives the highest mark he has given in an age. The worlds under him have a small earthquake of approval.

fail.log: You guess wrong. Ulsan begins his question again from the start, out of patience, which is worse.

events.text: The sun-gods set the Examination of the Book of Fates at noon, and their noon lasts as long as they like. The ink of the Examination is made from the candidates' own forgotten dreams. Halfway through the second paper yours runs dry. You have not been dreaming much. The proctor raises an eyebrow.

choices.text: Ask the proctor for more

effects.log: He gives you a pot from the common jar. Your answers come out in a stranger hand, full of other gods' dreams: a red fox, a falling tower. They read well.

choices.text: Close your eyes and dream something up

effects.log: You put your head on the desk and dream, on purpose, of the house you grew up in. The ink comes back dark and steady. You finish with tears on the page.

events.text: Candidates of the Will of Heaven sit in rows of light, and the Book is read aloud by a herald made of fire. A god of a minor pantheon finds you in the corridor. He offers you a whole world's harvest, a year of it, delivered in sheaves, if you sit the Examination in his son's name. His son is waiting outside, plainly hoping you refuse.

choices.text: Refuse, and say so in front of the son

effects.log: The father goes red. The son mouths thank you over his shoulder. A year later he comes to the exam himself and fails it honestly, and seems very happy.

choices.text: Refuse quietly, and report it

effects.log: The proctors thank you and say they get one of these every cycle. Your name goes on a short list of candidates they trust.

events.text: In the Will of Heaven the examination hall is lit from every side, so no candidate can hide a thought. The results go up on the wall of heaven. Your name is there, but spelled wrong. In the Book of Fates a misspelled name is a different god, with a different fate, and that god now exists, a little, somewhere.

choices.text: Have it corrected

effects.log: It takes three offices and a year. The other god, who never quite existed, is struck out. You feel oddly sorry for them.

choices.text: Go and find the other one

effects.log: The other fate is a quiet one: a small god of a well. For a while it follows you about like a stray. Then it finds its well, and you visit sometimes.

effects.log: The other fate is a quiet one: a small god of a well. For a while it follows you about like a stray. Then it finds its well, and you visit sometimes.

choices.text: Leave it; nobody is hurt

effects.log: Nobody is hurt. Those four hundred marriages turn out unusually long and well organised. The clerk is promoted by accident.

events.text: Your post in the Will of Heaven is in a hall with no shadows, so every clerk sees what every other is doing. Your desk-mate is Bongsu, god of tea leaves, who reads the fortune in every cup he drinks and drinks forty cups a day. Today, staring into the bottom of one, he goes pale and will not tell you what he saw.

choices.text: Make him tell you

effects.log: He tells you: your name, and a long journey, and a closed door. "It is only tea," he says, and drinks another, very quickly.

choices.text: Make him a cup yourself, and hide the leaves

effects.log: You make it with leaves strained out. He drinks it and has nothing to read for the first time in an age. He sits back and says it is wonderful.

events.text: In the courts of the sky the morning bell is a sunrise, and you are expected at your desk before it is over. A god of small mercies borrowed ten thousand prayers from the court's reserve in a lean century and never paid them back. You are sent to collect. He keeps a tiny shrine on a cold world, and they still pray to him, a little.

choices.text: Collect in full

effects.log: You collect. He goes very faint, and the cold world has a hard winter without his small mercies. The ledger is clean. You are commended.

choices.text: Write the debt down to what he can pay

effects.log: He pays a tenth and thanks you twice. Your superior grumbles at the figures. The cold world keeps its small mercies.

choices.text: Find the clause that forgives it

ok.log: There is a clause, written for lean centuries. The debt is struck out lawfully. He sends you a warm stone every winter.

fail.log: The clause is there but it expired an age ago. You have wasted a month, and the debt stands.

events.text: Fire-clerks of the Will of Heaven carry petitions that smoke a little, which means they are urgent. You share a watch at the lesser gate with Munji, a gatekeeper who has let nobody through for an age. Today a weary minor goddess with a sick world on her back asks to pass. Munji says the paperwork is not right. It is not.

choices.text: Let her through and sign for it yourself

effects.log: She goes through. You sign. Munji says nothing for a week, then admits he was waiting an age for someone to do that.

choices.text: Fill in the right paperwork for her, on the spot

effects.log: It takes all night. She goes through at dawn, properly stamped. Munji approves of you, and tells everyone.

events.text: Your post in the Will of Heaven is in a hall with no shadows, so every clerk sees what every other is doing. A mortal has climbed all the way up to {cth_court} to complain. Ongbae, a farmer, dusty and old, with a list. His village's prayers have gone unanswered for three years and he wants to know whose desk they are on. They are on yours.

choices.text: Apologise to his face and answer them now

effects.log: You answer three years of prayers in an afternoon, with him reading over your shoulder. He goes home on a cloud. He leaves the list. It has a rude drawing of you on it.

choices.text: Blame the backlog and the office

effects.log: He listens and nods and says that is what the tax man says too. He goes home on foot. The prayers get answered in time, but he does not pray to anyone again.

events.text: In the courts of the sky the morning bell is a sunrise, and you are expected at your desk before it is over. Your superior, Lord Jangsu, takes your report on the shifting of a world's seasons, puts his name on it, and presents it to the court. It is very well received. He thanks you warmly for your help with the copying.

choices.text: Let it go and write the next one better

effects.log: You write the next one better and send it up in your own hand, under his. The court notices the hand. Jangsu notices the court noticing.

choices.text: Ask him a question about it in front of the court

ok.log: He cannot answer. You can, smoothly, as if helping him. Everyone understands and nobody says so.

fail.log: He answers well enough, as if he wrote it, and you look like a junior who wanted attention.

events.text: Fire-clerks of the Will of Heaven carry petitions that smoke a little, which means they are urgent. A new star has kindled over a cluster of worlds and needs a name in the Book. A committee of nine is set to choose. They have met for forty years. The worlds below have started calling it Bob.

choices.text: Propose that it be called Bob

effects.log: There is uproar, then a vote, then a tie, then Bob. The worlds below are delighted. The committee will not speak to you for a century.

choices.text: Draft a short list of three and force a vote

effects.log: They pick the third, a long name meaning Lamp of Patience. The worlds keep calling it Bob anyway. The Book records both.

events.text: Your post in the Will of Heaven is in a hall with no shadows, so every clerk sees what every other is doing. A backlog in the dream office: six hundred years of undelivered dreams in sacks, some of them urgent warnings that are now history. The sacks keep muttering. The clerk in charge is asleep, which is ironic, and also his job.

choices.text: Deliver the useful ones, burn the stale

effects.log: You sort for a decade. Some warnings still matter; a few worlds dodge a flood thanks to a dream six centuries late.

choices.text: Wake the clerk and make it his problem

effects.log: He wakes, sorts a single sack and falls asleep on it. But he does deliver one dream: to you, of a long road, which you think about for some time.

events.text: In the upper halls of the Will of Heaven, a quarrel is settled by who is still visible at the end of it. {cth_Court} has split into two factions: those who want dawn to come a little earlier across the domain, and those who want dusk to come later. Nobody remembers why it matters. Both have offered you a seat.

choices.text: Join the dawn faction

events.text: In the upper halls of the Will of Heaven, a quarrel is settled by who is still visible at the end of it. The inner council proposes to let one world wither, to punish its priests for preaching another pantheon. It would be a slow thing: a few bad harvests, a few hundred years. The vote comes round the table to you.

choices.text: Vote against

effects.log: You lose the vote but slow it by a century. In that century the priests change their minds without being made to.

choices.text: Vote for, and propose it be gentle

effects.log: It passes, gentled. The harvests are thin, not bad. The priests come back. You wonder, after, if that was the same thing done kindly.

The council of {cth_court} sits on the boundary between night and evening, which has never been fixed. The session is in its ninetieth year. Several members have grown beards. choices.text: Propose a boundary and push it to a vote

effects.log: Your boundary passes in the ninety-third year. The worlds below notice nothing at all, but it is in the Book now, and that is your doing.

choices.text: Excuse yourself for a few decades

effects.log: You go and do something useful. When you come back the session has reached the topic of the boundary between evening and late evening.

events.text: The great lords of the sky sit in a ring of light, and they rank one another by how much of it they stand in. There is a motion to reform the spelling of the Book of Fates, which is very old and very strange. Spelling changes in the Book change fates. Under the new rules, about two million mortals would have slightly different lives.

choices.text: Support the reform

effects.log: It passes. Two million mortals have their lives nudged: an apple instead of a pear, a left turn for a right. The clerks are delighted.

choices.text: Oppose it on their behalf

effects.log: You speak for two million people who will never know. It fails. The clerks hate you for a thousand years.

events.text: In the upper halls of the Will of Heaven, a quarrel is settled by who is still visible at the end of it. Old Minister Haenim is retiring after an age at the right hand of {cth_throne}. She calls you into her rooms, which are full of half-packed boxes, and asks if you want her seat. She warns you it is mostly reading other people's complaints.

choices.text: Accept

effects.log: She gives you her seal and a list of everyone who will try to make you fail. The list is long and alphabetical.

choices.text: Ask her to name someone better

effects.log: She names a quiet clerk nobody thinks of. You back him. He is very good. He owes you for ever, and knows it.

events.text: High in the Will of Heaven, a seat near the throne is a seat in its glare, and nothing you do is unseen. A lord of a neighbouring pantheon sends you a jewel: a deep blue stone with something moving in it. Holding it to the light you see that it is a tiny god, trapped, beating against the facets.

choices.text: Break it open and let the god out

effects.log: A very small god of puddles unfolds and thanks you and runs away. The lord who sent it takes offence. You have an enemy and a puddle that likes you.

choices.text: Send it back with your thanks

effects.log: You send it back, untouched, with very polite thanks. The lord understands exactly what that means and is a little afraid of you.

events.text: The great lords of the sky sit in a ring of light, and they rank one another by how much of it they stand in. The prayer budget of {cth_court} is short this age, and one domain must be cut. The choice is between the god of lullabies and the god of lost things. Neither has many friends at court. Both are on the list in your hand.

choices.text: Cut lullabies

effects.log: The god of lullabies takes it gracefully. Across many worlds, children sleep a little worse. You hear it, somehow, at night.

choices.text: Cut lost things

effects.log: The god of lost things takes it badly. Keys go missing across a thousand worlds and stay missing. Including yours.

choices.text: Cut your own office instead

effects.log: You trim your own allowance and keep both. You live more plainly for an age. People notice, and it shames a few of them into doing the same.

An old friend from your examination year comes to you with her mother's fate line copied out. Her mother is a mortal and has three months. The Oath to the Book forbids you to touch a line. She does not ask. She just leaves the copy on your table.

choices.text: Leave it on the table

effects.log: It sits there for three months. On the last day you go with her to the mortal world and sit by the bed. The Oath holds. So does she, mostly.

effects.log: Three months becomes three years. The Book does not notice. You do, every day.

events.text: The Oath to the Book, under the Throne of Storms, is sworn on a mountain, which must then keep standing. An old friend from your examination year comes to you with her mother's fate line copied out. Her mother is a mortal and has three months. The Oath to the Book forbids you to touch a line. She does not ask. She just leaves the copy on your table.

choices.text: Leave it on the table

effects.log: It sits there for three months. On the last day you go with her to the mortal world and sit by the bed. The Oath holds. So does she, mostly.

events.text: Sun-gods swear in the open, at noon, so the oath has been seen by every world that looked up that day. Long ago you told the Book a small lie: you recorded a prayer as answered when it was only half answered. The Oath says never to lie to the Book. This century the Book has started underlining that entry in red.

choices.text: Go back and answer the rest of the prayer

effects.log: It was a widow asking for her son to come home. He came home lame. You go down and mend his leg, an age late, and the underline fades.

choices.text: Confess the lie to the Keepers

effects.log: They are surprised anybody confesses. You are fined a year of prayers. The underline stays, but it stops being red.

choices.text: Let it go and watch him

effects.log: You watch him for a century. He does nothing wrong. Perhaps it was only a slip. Perhaps he is careful.

events.text: The Oath to the Book, sworn under the Will of Heaven, is written in fire on the inside of your eyelids. {cth_ruler} orders you, quietly, to remove a rival god's name from one page of the Book, just one, for a single age. The Oath forbids it. The order is written in their own hand on fine paper.

choices.text: Refuse, and hand back the paper

effects.log: {cth_ruler} takes it back without a word. You are not punished. You are not asked to the long walk again, either.

choices.text: Obey

effects.log: You do it. The rival god spends an age forgotten, wandering. The Book shows a faint stain on that page. You do not look at it.

choices.text: Find a lawful way to give them what they want

ok.log: You find one: the rival can be sent on a very long honourable mission instead. Everyone is satisfied, and the Book stays clean.

fail.log: Your lawful way is lawful and useless. {cth_ruler} is disappointed in your cleverness.

events.text: Sun-gods swear in the open, at noon, so the oath has been seen by every world that looked up that day. The Oath is renewed every thousand years. Your wording is old: it binds you to the Book and to the worlds that pray, in that order. The new wording drops the worlds. Everyone else has signed.

choices.text: Sign the new wording

effects.log: It is a short ceremony and you are home in time for supper. The worlds below never knew they were in it.

choices.text: Swear the old wording, aloud, alone

effects.log: It takes longer and everyone stares. The Keepers write it down because they must. The worlds are still in it, in your oath at least.

events.text: In the Will of Heaven an oath you keep shines a little; one you bend leaves a mark like a burn. You come across a fate line in the Book: a mortal child named Sori will drown at seven, in a pond, on a sunny afternoon. The Oath forbids you to change it. It does not forbid you to be at the pond.

choices.text: Be at the pond

effects.log: You are a heron on the bank on that afternoon. Sori falls in. A heron is not a god. A heron can flap and shout. Her father comes running. The Book records a near thing.

choices.text: Respect the Book

effects.log: You do not go. You do not look at the page again. You think about it at every pond for a thousand years.

events.text: The Oath to the Book, sworn under the Will of Heaven, is written in fire on the inside of your eyelids. Your Oath has an old clause: you are bound to remember the god Ilmok, whom nobody else remembers. You do not know who Ilmok was. Every morning you say the name. If you stop, Ilmok ends.

choices.text: Find out who Ilmok was

effects.log: It takes decades. Ilmok was the god of the first word ever spoken in heaven. The word was "wait". You go on saying the name with more feeling.

choices.text: Keep saying it, and leave the rest alone

effects.log: Every morning, Ilmok. It becomes like breathing. Sometimes on a still morning you think something says thank you.

events.text: Sun-gods swear in the open, at noon, so the oath has been seen by every world that looked up that day. Sabeop, a god of contracts who wears seven pairs of spectacles, comes to your door with an offer. For a fee he can show you a clause that makes your Oath not apply on alternate Tuesdays. He has made a living from this for an age.

choices.text: Send him away

effects.log: He shrugs and goes next door. You hear the neighbour laughing. Tuesday becomes a strange day around the court.

choices.text: Pay to read the clause, not to use it

effects.log: It is a beautiful clause and quite real. You do not use it, but you report it, and it is struck out. Sabeop is out of business and sends you a curse in a very nice hand.

Swearing the Oath, you promised once to answer any question truthfully if it was asked at the Book's lectern. Today {cth_rival} stands at the lectern and asks you, in front of the court, what you really think of {cth_ruler}.

choices.text: Answer truthfully and kindly

choices.text: Answer truthfully and completely

effects.log: You say everything, the good and the long list of bad. The Book is satisfied. Nobody else is. {cth_rival} looks very happy.

events.text: The Oath to the Book, sworn under the Will of Heaven, is written in fire on the inside of your eyelids. A god has broken his Oath: he moved a single fate so that a drought fell on an empty desert instead of a full valley. He saved a valley. The law says he must be stripped of his domain. You are the judge.

choices.text: Strip him, as the law says

effects.log: He bows his head and goes. The law holds, and the valley lives. You will think about the shape of this case for a long time.

choices.text: Find him guilty and sentence him lightly

effects.log: A century of sweeping the steps of the Book. He sweeps them very well. Some say you made the Oath cheap. Some say you made it kind.

events.text: In the sky-courts a hymn is judged by how many worlds still sing it after the sun has set on them. One of your hymns has caught on in a world called Haesong, but they are singing it wrong. They have turned a hymn about patience into a drinking song, and it is enormously popular, and the priests are furious.

choices.text: Let them sing it their way

effects.log: It becomes the most-sung hymn in your works. Nobody remembers it was about patience. Everyone remembers the chorus.

choices.text: Send a dream to set them right

effects.log: You send the priests a dream of the proper tune. Half the world sings it your way, half theirs. They hold competitions.

events.text: The fire-poets of the Will of Heaven write in light, and their drafts fade if they are not finished by dusk. A great lord of {cth_court} offers to be your patron, on one condition: your next hymn is about him. He is not a very interesting god. His domain is the patience of queues.

choices.text: Write the hymn and make it good

effects.log: You find the poetry in queues: people waiting together, the small kindness of saving a place. It is surprisingly lovely. He weeps.

events.text: In the Will of Heaven a soldier of the Host is never off duty, because the sky is never off duty. Drill in {cth_legion}. The formation wheels left across the sky, and below it a world gets three days of rain it had not asked for. A farmer's prayer comes up, very cross, addressed to whoever was on the left flank. That was you.

choices.text: Answer the prayer and apologise

effects.log: You send the farmer a dry week and a note. The sergeant says this is not how the Host works. Within a century the whole left flank answers its own prayers.

choices.text: Drill harder so the wheel is tighter

effects.log: You drill until the wheel turns in a single heartbeat. The rain falls on an empty sea. The farmer has a dry week anyway, by luck.

events.text: In the Will of Heaven a soldier of the Host is never off duty, because the sky is never off duty. The Host's stables hold a celestial horse called Cheonma who has thrown every rider for an age. He is made of a summer wind and a bad temper. effects.log: He carries you as if you were nothing. You become known in the Host as the one Cheonma chose, which brings you envy and a great deal of extra duty.

effects.log: You groom him every morning. He follows you about like a dog. The stablemaster says it is the first time Cheonma has looked happy since the founding.

An order comes down for {cth_legion} to march straight across the sky of a world called Mulgok, to save three days. A march of the Host across a sky means a flood below. choices.text: Obey the order

effects.log: You march. Mulgok floods for a season. You save three days, and win nothing with them. You read the prayers that come up.

choices.text: Take the long way round, and answer for it

effects.log: You arrive three days late and are reprimanded in writing. Mulgok has a normal autumn and never knows how close it came.

choices.text: Send word up to have the order changed

ok.log: A sensible officer changes it. You go round without being late, as the new order allows.

fail.log: The officer is not sensible. You go round anyway, late, and you are now known as difficult.

Haesal, who joined the Host the same day as you, is hurt in drill: a bolt of light went the wrong way. The healers say she will mend in a century, but she must leave the Host. effects.log: She is angry for ten years. Then she writes to say she has a domain of her own now, a small hillside of morning light. She seems to like it.

events.text: A general of the Will of Heaven rides a chariot of noon, and draws every plan where the enemy can see it. You hold the Gate of Dusk at the edge of the domain: a fortress built on the line where evening becomes night. It is cold, quiet, and in the wrong place. Since it was built, the evening has crept a mile to the east.

choices.text: Move the fortress to the new line

effects.log: It takes a century to move. The engineers grumble all the way. When it is done the line stops creeping, as if the fortress had been holding it.

choices.text: Hold the old line

effects.log: You hold the old line. The evening is, you notice, slightly confused by this. It creeps back an inch a year to meet you.

choices.text: Assume a trap and do the opposite

effects.log: You do the opposite. It works. The cartographer, it turns out, was bored. You have the map framed.

choices.text: Send it back with corrections

effects.log: You send it back with corrections in red ink, very politely. The enemy general writes back. You begin a correspondence that lasts the whole war.

events.text: A general of the Will of Heaven rides a chariot of noon, and draws every plan where the enemy can see it. {cth_rival} has been given the command beside yours and has not spoken to you in ten years. Your two wings must move together tomorrow. Neither of you has sent the other the plan.

choices.text: Ride over tonight and swallow your pride

effects.log: You ride over. {cth_rival} is sitting in the dark with the same map, waiting for you to come. You plan it together till dawn and it goes perfectly.

choices.text: Send your plan by a messenger

effects.log: You send yours; {cth_rival} sends theirs. They do not agree. Both wings move anyway. It is a messy day, and neither of you will admit it.

events.text: The sun-marshals hold that a war is won by being seen to win it, and they keep painters on the staff. An order from {cth_court}: give up the mountain pass you have held for twenty years. The pass guards a world called Byeolmok, which prays to your pantheon. If you go, {cth_foe} takes it in a week.

choices.text: Obey and retreat

effects.log: You retreat in good order. Byeolmok changes its prayers within the year. You keep a list of the names of its temples.

choices.text: Hold the pass and argue by letter

effects.log: You hold it and write a very long letter. By the time it is answered the war has moved on and Byeolmok is safe. You are reprimanded by the court and thanked by the world.

events.text: Your banners in the Will of Heaven burn without being consumed, which is fine until it rains. A god of {cth_foe}'s Host walks into your camp at night and surrenders. Her name is Saetbyeol. She says she is tired of the war and wants to go home to her little domain, a pond of morning mist, and look after it.

choices.text: Let her go home

effects.log: You give her a pass. The pond of morning mist stays out of the war for its whole length, and some of your soldiers rest there on leave.

choices.text: Keep her for questioning first

effects.log: She tells you useful things, kindly, because she wants it to be over. You win a battle with them. Then you let her go home.

events.text: A general of the Will of Heaven rides a chariot of noon, and draws every plan where the enemy can see it. The battle is in the weather. Your wing is a front of high pressure, the enemy a cold low, and below you a world is getting hail the size of apples. Your officers ask for orders.

choices.text: Push hard and finish it

effects.log: The low breaks and runs. The hail stops. The world below has had the worst storm in its history, but it is over by teatime.

choices.text: Draw off and fight tomorrow, elsewhere

effects.log: You draw off. The world below has a pleasant afternoon. The enemy thinks you have lost your nerve, and you let them.

events.text: The sun-marshals hold that a war is won by being seen to win it, and they keep painters on the staff. Your youngest officer, Jinu, god of a single bright morning, is brave to the point of foolishness. Today he charged a ridge alone and took it. He is pleased with himself. It nearly lost you the wing.

choices.text: Praise him in front of the Host

effects.log: He glows. He charges three more ridges in the next ten years, two of them sensibly.

choices.text: Reprimand him in private

effects.log: He takes it badly and then takes it to heart. He becomes the steadiest officer you have, and never tells anyone why.

events.text: Your banners in the Will of Heaven burn without being consumed, which is fine until it rains. Your supply comes through a world called Gamnam, whose people are asked to send up extra prayers to keep the Host fed. They are poor and their harvests are bad. The prayers are getting thinner.

choices.text: Put the Host on short rations

effects.log: The Host grumbles but holds. Gamnam is let alone and its harvests recover. Your soldiers are leaner and somehow prouder.

choices.text: Take what the Host needs

effects.log: You take it. Gamnam keeps praying, thinner every year. You win your war, and the people of Gamnam are hungry for a long time.

choices.text: Approve all eighty-one

effects.log: Eighty are brilliant. One makes all the rivers run uphill on rest days. Nuri is thrilled. The domain prospers, mostly.

choices.text: Read every one and approve forty

effects.log: It takes a year. Nuri is disappointed and also, secretly, relieved: forty is plenty. The domain improves steadily.

events.text: Your lesser domain under the Will of Heaven is a small sky over a few worlds, who look up at it every day. events.text: A fief of the sky-gods comes with a duty to be seen, so your domain's dawn is never allowed to be late. A flood has come to Jangmal, a world in {cth_fief}. It is not your fault: a storm-god upstream let a sea slip. But the people of Jangmal pray to you, and they want it to stop.

choices.text: Go down and hold the water back

effects.log: You stand in the flood for three days with your arms out. It goes down. You come back up soaked and tired and much more loved.

choices.text: Write to the storm-god upstream

effects.log: He apologises, by weather, and the flood stops in a week. Jangmal is grateful but slightly disappointed in you.

choices.text: Open a new river to drain it

ok.log: A new river runs out of the plain to the sea. Jangmal names it after you, which is embarrassing.

choices.text: Go down and hold the water back

effects.log: You stand in the flood for three days with your arms out. It goes down. You come back up soaked and tired and much more loved.

choices.text: Write to the storm-god upstream

effects.log: He apologises, by weather, and the flood stops in a week. Jangmal is grateful but slightly disappointed in you.

events.text: A fief of the sky-gods comes with a duty to be seen, so your domain's dawn is never allowed to be late. Famine in a world of {cth_fief}. The priests are offering up their own last grain, which is the worst kind of prayer: very strong, and it costs them everything.

choices.text: Refuse the offering and send it back

effects.log: You send it back with interest. The world eats. You are thin for a decade, but you sleep.

choices.text: Accept it and answer it

effects.log: You accept and answer. The famine ends, but the priests remember the price. They pray to you more carefully after.

events.text: Your lesser domain under the Will of Heaven is a small sky over a few worlds, who look up at it every day. A new world has been born in {cth_fief}, small and hot and shapeless, like a lump of dough. It has no people yet. Your steward asks what kind of world you want it to be.

choices.text: Make it a quiet world

effects.log: You make it gentle, with long evenings and slow rivers. When people come to it they are a calm sort, and write good poetry.

choices.text: Let it decide for itself

effects.log: You leave it alone. It decides to be a world of very tall mountains and very small, very determined goats. You are oddly proud.

The priests have the plans ready: three days, lanterns, a great deal of rice wine. The cost to the poorer worlds is high.

choices.text: Allow it yearly, and pay for the poor worlds

effects.log: It costs you a great deal and your hall is shabby again. But every year the lanterns go up, and you can see them from your window.

The seating was arranged by a god of precedence who ended an age ago. Nobody dares change it. You are next to the god of colds.

effects.log: He is shy and lovely and never invited anywhere. You leave with a sniffle and a friend for life.

choices.text: Change the seating, quietly

effects.log: You swap two cards and sit beside an old lord who matters. Nobody says anything. Everybody notices.

events.text: The peers of the Will of Heaven meet in a hall where the light shows every crease in a robe and every lie. A great house of {cth_court} offers you a consort from their line, to bind your houses. The young god in question writes you a private letter: they would prefer not to, but will do their duty.

choices.text: Accept the alliance as a formality

effects.log: You accept. You live in separate halls and become, in time, good friends. The bond between the houses holds through two wars.

events.text: A title in the Throne of Storms comes with a storm of your own, and the peers judge one another by noise. Lord Hwangso, an old peer, says in the hall that your house was made yesterday out of nothing. It is true. Several peers wait to see what you will do.

choices.text: Agree with him, warmly

effects.log: You agree you were made of nothing, and thank him for remembering. Hwangso does not know what to do with this. Neither does anyone else.

events.text: Among the sky-lords, rank is how high your seat is set against the sun, and the stairs are long. The house of Seolha, once the greatest in {cth_court}, has dwindled to one old god in one room of a ruined hall, waiting for his last worshipper to stop praying. He invites you to tea. The teapot is chipped.

choices.text: Go to tea every month

effects.log: He tells you everything about the court as it was. When his last worshipper stops praying, you begin, and he stays.

choices.text: Go once, and offer him a post

effects.log: He is offended: he was the greatest house in the court. But he takes the post, and he is very good at it.

events.text: The peers of the Will of Heaven meet in a hall where the light shows every crease in a robe and every lie. As {cth_title} you sign what the throne decides. Today {cth_ruler} decides that a world which has stopped praying should be given to {cth_foe}. Your signature is needed.

choices.text: Sign

effects.log: You sign. The world goes to {cth_foe}. Its people pray to new gods and are, perhaps, no worse off.

choices.text: Ask for a year to visit the world first

effects.log: You visit and find out why it stopped: its god ended and nobody told them. You become its god yourself. It stays.

events.text: A title in the Will of Heaven comes with a halo of a set width, and the peers measure one another's. The peers' great hunt. The quarry is a comet, fast and bright and never caught. The hounds are made of wind. The comet has been running from this hunt for nine thousand years.

choices.text: Ride to catch it

effects.log: You catch it. It is small and frightened and warm in your hands. Everyone cheers. You let it go when nobody is looking.

choices.text: Hang back and let it run

effects.log: You lose sight of the hunt. The comet slows down beside you and keeps you company for a while.

A whisper goes round the peers of {cth_court}: that you were once mortal, and that you still remember the people who raised you. Here it is a mild scandal to remember anyone mortal. Several peers are watching your face.

choices.text: Say it is true

effects.log: You say yes, and that she made the best soup in her village. The court is scandalised for a week. Then several peers privately admit they remember theirs.

choices.text: Say nothing

effects.log: You say nothing and the whisper dies down. You go home and remember her anyway.

events.text: The throne of the Will of Heaven stands empty, and a throne in that hall still casts no shadow. The heir to {cth_throne} is a very young god who likes to turn clouds into animals. You are regent until the heir is grown, which in this realm is about four thousand years. The heir asks every morning whether it is time yet.

choices.text: Teach the heir to rule

effects.log: Lessons every day. The heir learns slowly and well, and the cloud animals get better too. The realm trusts you more for the patience.

choices.text: Let the heir play, and rule alone

effects.log: You rule alone, efficiently. The heir grows up making animals, and you wonder later if you missed something.

events.text: As regent of the sky you sit beside the empty seat, in its glare, and every world below sees you squint. The council of {cth_court} is meeting without you. A servant tells you. They are discussing whether a regent is really needed, or whether a council of nine would do as well.

choices.text: Walk in uninvited

effects.log: You walk in and sit down. The council goes quiet. You listen to the rest of the meeting without a word. Nobody brings it up again.

choices.text: Win them over one by one

effects.log: You meet each of the nine alone over the next decade. By the end, seven are on your side and two are confused.

choices.text: Offer to share power with them

effects.log: They are surprised, and accept. The realm runs more slowly and more fairly. Your hand is weaker, but steadier.

effects.log: You move the Host to the river. {cth_foe} withdraws its letter. The realm feels safer and you feel very tired.

choices.text: Give them half the river

effects.log: They are pleased. Your court is furious, and the realm's trust in you falls.

events.text: The sun-gods do not like an empty throne. It looks like an eclipse, and eclipses frighten the worlds. The heir's tutor, Baram, a god of the north wind, has been teaching the heir that regents always steal the throne in the end. The heir is now very polite to you, and watchful.

choices.text: Dismiss the tutor

effects.log: Baram goes. The heir is upset, and more watchful than before.

choices.text: Tell the heir it is a fair worry

effects.log: You agree it is a fair worry, and show the heir the day you will hand over, written in the Book. The heir stops watching you.

A petitioner has been in audience before {cth_throne} for a century: the god of a small archipelago, making a very thorough case for one more island. He has reached the fourth of nine points. The court is asleep.

choices.text: Grant the island now, to end it

effects.log: He is delighted and a little disappointed: he had a lovely ninth point. The court wakes. Every lesser god in the realm learns that long petitions work.

choices.text: Hear him out to the end

effects.log: Points five to nine take another century. The ninth point is lovely. You grant him two islands, and the realm decides its ruler is patient.

events.text: From the throne of the Will of Heaven you are seen by every world that has a sky, which is most of them. {cth_Court} expects you to take a consort, and there are three: Lady Hanbit, who brings an army; Lord Seori, who brings a library; and Ongdal, a quiet god of a mountain spring, who brings nothing and makes you laugh.

choices.text: Hanbit and the army

effects.log: The realm is safer for an age. Hanbit is brisk and loyal, and you respect each other very much.

choices.text: Seori and the library

effects.log: Your court becomes the most learned in heaven. Seori reads aloud to you in the evenings, which you did not know you needed.

choices.text: Ongdal, for no good reason

effects.log: The court is aghast. The realm is charmed. You laugh more in the next age than in all the ages before it.

events.text: On the sun-throne an audience is held at noon, and noon waits until you are finished. Two gods stand before {cth_throne}: the god of a river and the god of the sea it runs into. Each claims the delta. Its three hundred villages have each built a shrine to both, to be safe.

choices.text: Split the delta down the middle

effects.log: Both gods sulk. The villages go on praying to both. It is fair and pleases nobody, which the old judges say is the sign.

choices.text: Let the villages choose

effects.log: Every village chooses both. You make it law. The two gods have to share, and slowly come to like it.

choices.text: Make the two gods sit together until they agree

ok.log: It takes forty years. They agree, and by the end are consorts. The delta floods beautifully every spring.

fail.log: They do not agree, and flood the delta in a temper. You send the villages a dry year by way of apology.

events.text: The worlds below the Will of Heaven light fires to you each dusk; their smoke is the tribute that rises. A world called Chorok is in famine and praying with all its strength. You could end it with a thought. But Chorok's priests have preached rising against {cth_throne} for a century.

choices.text: End the famine anyway

effects.log: You end it. Chorok's priests are confused, then ashamed. Some keep preaching; the people stop listening.

choices.text: Let it run a season, then end it

effects.log: One hungry season; you end it on the first day of spring. They learn the lesson. They also learn to fear you, and fear is a thin kind of prayer.

events.text: Out of the glare of the Will of Heaven at last, you find that you cast a shadow again, and you like it. You keep a garden now, on a quiet edge of the domain, and grow small blue flowers that have no use at all. Once a decade an old minister climbs up to ask your advice. You give it while weeding.

effects.log: He goes away with it. You find you are glad to be asked, and glad to be left alone after. The flowers spread.

effects.log: It is a kind lie. It does not get lighter, and they find that out. They forgive you, and bring you a better kettle.

events.text: Out of the glare of the Will of Heaven at last, you find that you cast a shadow again, and you like it. {cth_rival} comes to your gate, old now and also out of office. You fought each other for a thousand ages. They have brought a bottle and want to talk about the old days.

effects.log: You talk till dawn. It turns out you were each right about some things, and that you liked each other all along. It is a long, foolish, happy night.

choices.text: Send them away

effects.log: They go without arguing, which is not like them. You regret it a little, and do not send after them.

events.text: Old sun-gods retire to the evening, where the light is long and kinder and nobody needs them at noon. A young god knocks at your gate and asks to learn from you. Her name is Seulgi. She is clever, rude and impatient, and she reminds you very much of someone.

effects.log: You teach her everything. She is ungrateful and brilliant. One day she will sit somewhere high, and you hope you taught her the part about listening.

choices.text: Send her to a better teacher

effects.log: You send her to the god of the long road. She writes every century to complain about him. You enjoy the letters more than anything.

effects.log: You find it a misty world with a great many hills. It goes. Some autumns it comes back to sit by your door.

events.text: From the throne of the Will of Heaven you are seen by every world that has a sky, which is most of them. Your astronomers report that an eclipse is due over four hundred worlds that pray to {cth_throne}. It is only the sky doing sums. But four hundred priesthoods are already writing sermons about what you must be angry about.

choices.text: Send word ahead that it means nothing

effects.log: You send a dream to every priesthood. Most believe it. A few preach that a ruler who explains eclipses has something to hide.

choices.text: Let it pass, and answer the frightened prayers after

effects.log: The eclipse comes. You answer a great flood of frightened prayers, one by one, for a year. Four hundred worlds decide you are merciful.

choices.text: Move the moon a hair, so it misses

effects.log: It misses. Astronomers in four hundred worlds tear up their tables and are furious with you for an age.

events.text: On the sun-throne an audience is held at noon, and noon waits until you are finished. The god who forged the crown of {cth_throne} an age ago, an old smith called Mundol, asks for an audience. He wants it back for a week. There is a flaw in it he has thought about every night since, and he cannot rest.

choices.text: Lend it to him

effects.log: You rule a week bareheaded. The court is scandalised. Mundol mends the flaw, weeps, and sleeps for a century. The crown sits better.

choices.text: Refuse; the crown is not a pot to mend

effects.log: He bows and goes. You notice the flaw yourself after that, a hair of a line, every morning in the mirror.

events.text: The worlds below the Will of Heaven light fires to you each dusk; their smoke is the tribute that rises. A poor world sends its tribute of the age: one prayer. A single long, careful prayer from a whole people, for a well that will not run dry. The treasurer wants it sent back as an insult.

choices.text: Answer it, and grant the well

effects.log: The well never runs dry. That world prays to you for ever after, all of it, every day. It becomes the richest tribute you have.

choices.text: Record it with the rest, and say nothing

effects.log: It sits in the ledger, one prayer among millions. The well runs dry in a hard summer. You find you remember the shape of the prayer.

events.text: The night before the Examination of the Book of Fates, a candidate called Myoseon asks you to check her practice copy of a page. She was once the small god of a fishing village. Beside her copy lies the true page, and one line on it is in her hand: a village that was written to drown in a spring flood now "sees the water turn". Pung, the little god of the reading-room ink, sees you see it.

choices.text: Ask her about it, quietly

effects.log: She tells you without crying: forty boats, a school, her grandmother's house. She wrote the line the year she rose. "Nobody was hurt," she says. "Nobody at all. That is the whole crime." Pung pretends to fill an inkwell.

choices.text: Pretend you saw nothing

effects.log: You talk about the weather. Myoseon thanks you for the help, very carefully. Pung looks at you for a long time and then goes back to his wells.

events.text: The third paper of the Examination. Examiner Saebyeok, an old goddess with ink-stained cuffs, sets each candidate a page of the Book and says: one line on it is forged; find it. Your page is the page. Myoseon sits two rows ahead, very still. Saebyeok is watching you, not the page.

choices.text: Mark the forged line

effects.log: You mark it. Saebyeok reads your paper and closes her eyes for a moment. "Correct," she says, and nothing else. Myoseon does not turn round.

choices.text: Mark a harmless slip of the pen instead

effects.log: There is a real slip, an old one, a lake spelled as a lane. You mark that. Saebyeok reads it, looks at you over her cuffs, and passes you.

choices.text: Write that the page is true as it stands

ok.log: You argue that a fate the Book has kept for a hundred years is the Book's own. Saebyeok reads it twice. "Interesting," she says, and passes you, and keeps your paper.

fail.log: Saebyeok reads it once. "That is not an answer," she says, "it is a confession on someone's behalf." You pass, barely.

events.text: Pung, the ink-god, comes to your door with his hat in his hands. The Keepers have opened an inquiry into the reading-room ink, because ink that writes on the Book should never be lent. It was his ink. If no one else is named, he will lose the wells he has kept for nine thousand years.

choices.text: Go before the Keepers and speak for Pung

effects.log: You tell the Keepers the ink was taken, not lent. They believe you, mostly. Pung keeps his wells. The inquiry, having lost one name, goes looking for another.

choices.text: Let the inquiry run its course

effects.log: You stay out of it. Pung is fined a thousand years of ink and keeps his wells, just. He stops saying good morning. The inquiry goes on looking.

events.text: The third paper of the Examination. Examiner Saebyeok, an old goddess with ink-stained cuffs, sets each candidate a page of the Book and says: one line on it is forged; find it. Your page is the page. Myoseon sits two rows ahead, very still. Saebyeok is watching you, not the page.

choices.text: Mark the forged line

effects.log: You mark it. Saebyeok reads your paper and closes her eyes for a moment. "Correct," she says, and nothing else. Myoseon does not turn round.

choices.text: Mark a harmless slip of the pen instead

effects.log: There is a real slip, an old one, a lake spelled as a lane. You mark that. Saebyeok reads it, looks at you over her cuffs, and passes you.

choices.text: Write that the page is true as it stands

ok.log: You argue that a fate the Book has kept for a hundred years is the Book's own. Saebyeok reads it twice. "Interesting," she says, and passes you, and keeps your paper.

fail.log: Saebyeok reads it once. "That is not an answer," she says, "it is a confession on someone's behalf." You pass, barely.

events.text: Pung, the ink-god, comes to your door with his hat in his hands. The Keepers have opened an inquiry into the reading-room ink, because ink that writes on the Book should never be lent. It was his ink. If no one else is named, he will lose the wells he has kept for nine thousand years.

choices.text: Go before the Keepers and speak for Pung

effects.log: You tell the Keepers the ink was taken, not lent. They believe you, mostly. Pung keeps his wells. The inquiry, having lost one name, goes looking for another.

choices.text: Let the inquiry run its course

effects.log: You stay out of it. Pung is fined a thousand years of ink and keeps his wells, just. He stops saying good morning. The inquiry goes on looking.

events.text: The night before the Examination of the Book of Fates, a candidate called Myoseon asks you to check her practice copy of a page. She was once the small god of a fishing village. Beside her copy lies the true page, and one line on it is in her hand: a village that was written to drown in a spring flood now "sees the water turn". Pung, the little god of the reading-room ink, sees you see it.

choices.text: Ask her about it, quietly

effects.log: She tells you without crying: forty boats, a school, her grandmother's house. She wrote the line the year she rose. "Nobody was hurt," she says. "Nobody at all. That is the whole crime." Pung pretends to fill an inkwell.

events.text: Myoseon stands before the Keepers of the Book, and Saebyeok asks you to stand witness, since it was your answer that found the line. If the line is struck, the village is written to drown again, a hundred years late. Myoseon looks at you once. "Say what you saw," she says. "I would."

choices.text: Say what you saw, and ask that the village be spared

ok.log: The Keepers strike Myoseon from the court, and let the village keep its line. "The Book is clean," Saebyeok says. "The sea can manage the rest." It is a hard mercy and a real one.

fail.log: The line is struck and the village written back to the flood. Saebyeok, white to the lips, sends you down to warn it. You get them onto the hills in time. Not the boats.

choices.text: Say what you saw, and nothing more

effects.log: The law runs on its own. The line is struck. You hear later that Saebyeok went down herself, on her own time, and moved forty boats up the beach the night before.

events.text: Years on, you go down to the fishing village. It is still there. There is a shrine on the headland to a small goddess nobody upstairs remembers, and a newer one beside it, to an old woman with ink-stained cuffs. Someone has left a pot of ink at both.

choices.text: Leave a prayer at both shrines

effects.log: You leave a prayer at each. On the way back up you meet Pung on the road with an inkpot, going the same way. He says good morning, for the first time in years.

choices.text: Write Myoseon's name back into the Book, in the margin

effects.log: Not a fate, only a name: the margin is allowed. It is very small. The next time you look, someone has underlined it.

events.text: Myoseon passed, and is now a junior clerk of the Book. The auditors are coming next month, the faceless ones. She asks you for nothing. She only tells you the date, and which shelf her page is on, and goes back to her desk with her hands shaking a little.

choices.text: Move the page to a shelf they already checked

effects.log: You do it at night. The auditors pass the shelf. You have now forged something too: not a fate, only a shelf mark. It is surprising how heavy a shelf mark is.

choices.text: Tell her she must go to Saebyeok herself

effects.log: She goes white, then goes. You do not know what is said. Myoseon keeps her post. Saebyeok, the next week, asks you to tea and talks only about fishing.

events.text: Saebyeok retires. At her leaving feast she finds you by the door, a cup in her hand. "I knew about the line the day she wrote it," she says. "I set it in the paper to see who would find it, and what they would do." She drinks. "Most people would like a test to have one answer."

choices.text: Ask her what the right answer was

effects.log: "There was a village," she says, "and there was a Book. You were the answer." She gives you her ink-stained cuffs, wrapped in paper, and goes down to the sea.

choices.text: Ask her why she never struck the line

effects.log: "Because I was examined once, too," says Saebyeok, and will not say more. Myoseon, across the room, raises her cup to you both.

events.text: {cth_ruler} has gone into the long sleep that old gods go into, and the will names you regent for the heir, Dalbit: a god of moonlight, small enough to sit in the seat sideways. Chancellor Okgyeong reads the will aloud in a dry voice. Afterwards the steward Gwangmu hands you the seal, and murmurs that there is a second page, and nobody needs to read it.

choices.text: Read the second page aloud to the court

effects.log: It says that if the heir is not ready when grown, the regent shall choose another. The court goes very quiet. Gwangmu smiles at the floor. Okgyeong writes it down.

choices.text: Read it alone, and keep it

effects.log: It says that if the heir is not ready when grown, the regent shall choose another. You fold it into your sleeve. Gwangmu looks pleased, which you do not like at all.

events.text: Dalbit has run away from lessons and is hiding under the empty throne. Because Dalbit is moonlight, a thousand worlds below are having moonlight at noon, and their priests are in a panic. Okgyeong stands at the foot of the dais with a lesson book. Gwangmu suggests a firm hand.

choices.text: Crawl under the throne and sit with Dalbit

effects.log: It is dusty under there. Dalbit says the throne is too big and the lessons are about dead people. You agree on both points. You come out together, and the worlds get their noon back.

choices.text: Order Dalbit out, firmly

effects.log: Dalbit comes out at once, with a face like a closed door. The worlds get their noon. Gwangmu nods approvingly. Okgyeong does not.

choices.text: Change the lessons

effects.log: You throw out the book of dead rulers and teach Dalbit about the worlds that pray: their names, their weather, their children. Dalbit learns every name in a year.

events.text: Gwangmu makes his move. Before the council he proposes that the regency be made permanent "until the heir proves ready", which would be when you say so. He has the votes. He turns to you, smiling, the second page in his hand. Okgyeong has taken off her chancellor's chain and laid it on the table.

choices.text: Accept the regency for as long as needed

effects.log: The council votes it. You hold the seat in all but name. Okgyeong leaves the hall without her chain. Dalbit, at the window, hears all of it.

choices.text: Refuse, and dismiss Gwangmu

effects.log: You tear the second page and hand Gwangmu the pieces. He bows very low and leaves by the far door, the one to the road that runs toward {cth_foe}. Okgyeong puts her chain back on.

events.text: Dalbit is grown now, and is no longer a child of moonlight but a cold clear night. Every year Dalbit asks you the same question, in the same voice, in front of the whole court: is it time yet? Every year the council waits for your answer. This year Dalbit has brought a written list of everything you have got wrong.

choices.text: Read the list aloud, and name a day

effects.log: It is a fair list. You read every line of it, and name a day a hundred years off. Dalbit says nothing, but folds the list away instead of tearing it.

choices.text: Say: not yet

effects.log: "Not yet," you say. The court looks at its shoes. Somewhere in the worlds below, a whole country starts sleeping badly, for no reason they can name.

events.text: The day comes, or it is taken. Dalbit sits {cth_throne} at last, and the first thing the new ruler does is look at you for a long time. Gwangmu, old now, is in the crowd, waiting to see if you will be thanked or thrown down.

choices.text: Kneel first, before the whole court

effects.log: You kneel first. It is not easy, and the knees of a god who has held a throne are stiff. Dalbit lets you kneel a moment longer than needed, then lifts you, and does not let go of your hand.

choices.text: Hand over the seal and leave by the side door

effects.log: You leave the seal on the arm of the throne and go. You are not thanked. You are not thrown down. A century later a letter comes, in Dalbit's hand: you were not wrong about everything.

effects.log: It is a fair list. You read every line of it, and name a day a hundred years off. Dalbit says nothing, but folds the list away instead of tearing it.

choices.text: Say: not yet

effects.log: "Not yet," you say. The court looks at its shoes. Somewhere in the worlds below, a whole country starts sleeping badly, for no reason they can name.

events.text: The day comes, or it is taken. Dalbit sits {cth_throne} at last, and the first thing the new ruler does is look at you for a long time. Gwangmu, old now, is in the crowd, waiting to see if you will be thanked or thrown down.

choices.text: Kneel first, before the whole court

effects.log: You kneel first. It is not easy, and the knees of a god who has held a throne are stiff. Dalbit lets you kneel a moment longer than needed, then lifts you, and does not let go of your hand.

choices.text: Hand over the seal and leave by the side door

effects.log: You leave the seal on the arm of the throne and go. You are not thanked. You are not thrown down. A century later a letter comes, in Dalbit's hand: you were not wrong about everything.

choices.text: Publish the true story yourself, first

effects.log: You tell the court and the worlds everything: the page, the tearing, the reason. It is a small scandal and then it is a story people like. Gwangmu's letter arrives in every world a month too late.

choices.text: Have Okgyeong prove the copy a forgery

ok.log: Okgyeong finds his steward's hand in a downstroke. The copy is shown up as Gwangmu's work. He is not welcome at {cth_foe}'s table after that.

fail.log: The copy is too good. Okgyeong cannot prove it false, and the rumour has a long, slow life.

events.text: Dalbit is crowned. In the procession the moonlight is so bright that a thousand worlds have the clearest night they have ever had, and stay up late on their roofs to look. Okgyeong walks beside you, chain and all. "You did not choose another," she says. "Most would have. It was right there on the page."

choices.text: Say there was never a second page

effects.log: "Of course," says Okgyeong, and almost smiles. Dalbit, from the head of the procession, turns and waves at you, which is not in the ceremony at all.

choices.text: Say you thought about it every day

effects.log: "Good," says Okgyeong. "Then you were the right regent." She makes you walk the rest of the way at Dalbit's right hand, against all the rules of precedence.

events.text: Jeokho, a god of small fires that keep travellers warm, comes to your rooms at night with a folded banner under his coat. The small gods are starving, he says: the tribute goes up and never comes down. He wants a throne that answers. He asks you to carry their demands to {cth_ruler}, since you have the ear. Or to carry the banner.

choices.text: Carry the demands to {cth_ruler}

effects.log: You carry them. {cth_ruler} reads every line, says they will be considered, and sets them on a pile. You see the pile. It has been there an age.

choices.text: Hear him out, promise nothing

effects.log: You hear all of it. You promise nothing. Jeokho goes back out into the dark, and leaves you a coal that never cools, in case you change your mind.

choices.text: Tell your friend General Seoknam

effects.log: You tell Seoknam, who has been your friend since your first post. He thanks you, gravely, and says that is the end of it. It is not the end of it.

events.text: The Godfall Banner goes up over a cold world on the edge of the domain. Mire, the rising's quartermaster, a goddess of orchards with dirt on her knees, comes to you in secret. Her orchard-worlds pray to the banner now. The throne will find out. She asks you to hide their prayers in your own accounts.

choices.text: Hide them

effects.log: You hide them, a few thousand prayers in the ledger of a high office. It is the best-kept secret in heaven for a year, and the worst thing you have ever done to a ledger.

choices.text: Refuse, and warn her to stop

effects.log: Mire says she cannot stop: they are her worlds. She leaves you a basket of plums. They are very good. You eat them all, feeling dreadful.

events.text: Seoknam is ordered to break the rising, and rides to your door in armour that has not been worn in an age. "Ride with me," he says. "You know them. You can end it with fewer hurt." That night there is a coal glowing on your windowsill that never cools. Jeokho is asking too.

choices.text: Ride with Seoknam

effects.log: You ride with him under the throne's banners. Seoknam is quiet and grateful. Behind you, the coal on the windowsill goes out.

choices.text: Go to Jeokho and the banner

effects.log: You go out at night with the coal in your hand. By morning you are under the Godfall Banner, and Seoknam is riding alone.

events.text: The rising breaks on the field below a cold world, and Jeokho is brought to Seoknam's tent in chains of light. He does not look surprised to see you. Seoknam, tired to the bone, says the prisoner is yours to judge: you knew him. Mire is not among the captured.

choices.text: Ask that Jeokho go before {cth_court}, and speak for him there

effects.log: You speak for an hour. Jeokho is not ended; he is bound to a single hearth for an age, which is his domain made very small. He thanks you for the hearth.

choices.text: Let the law take him

effects.log: The law takes him. Seoknam does not look at you for a while. It was the order. It was also your friend's order, and you had a choice.

events.text: After the rising, the orchard-worlds stop praying at all. Mire has gone to ground somewhere in them, and their trees are bare. Seoknam comes to you with a report: the small gods are still hungry, banner or no banner. "We won," he says. "I do not know what."

choices.text: Take Jeokho's demands to {cth_ruler} again, in your own name

effects.log: You take them yourself. Half of them are granted, under your name, which is a strange reward for the one who rode against them. The orchards bloom the next spring.

choices.text: Find Mire and make your peace

effects.log: It takes a decade. You find her in a bare orchard, pruning. She lets you hold the ladder. By the end of the season the trees have leaves.

events.text: You stand under the Godfall Banner on the field. Across it is Seoknam, at the head of the throne's Host, in his old armour. Before the lines close he rides out alone, to the middle, and waits. Jeokho tells you not to go. Mire hands you a plum for the road.

choices.text: Ride out and talk to him

effects.log: You talk in the middle of the field for an hour, while both armies watch. Neither of you gives way. When you ride back, the battle is smaller and shorter than anyone had planned.

choices.text: Hold the line when the Host comes

ok.log: The line holds. The Host draws off. Seoknam salutes you across the field, and the small gods sing all night.

fail.log: The line bends and nearly breaks. You hold the gap yourself until dark. The rising survives the day, and so, just, do you.

events.text: The banner reaches the doors of {cth_court}. Jeokho turns to you: you have the ear, he says, so you speak. The great hall is full. {cth_ruler} sits very still. Seoknam stands at the foot of the throne, unarmed now, waiting to hear what the rising wants.

choices.text: Ask for the tribute to come down as well as up

events.text: The banner reaches the doors of {cth_court}. Jeokho turns to you: you have the ear, he says, so you speak. The great hall is full. {cth_ruler} sits very still. Seoknam stands at the foot of the throne, unarmed now, waiting to hear what the rising wants.

choices.text: Ask for the tribute to come down as well as up

effects.log: One law, short. It passes in an age, which is fast here. The small gods grow solid again. Jeokho goes home to keep travellers warm, which is all he ever wanted.

choices.text: Ask for a seat for the small gods in the council

effects.log: One seat, for a god of wells. It is a beginning. Seoknam is the first to bow to the new councillor. Mire takes the seat, with dirt on her knees.

events.text: A small god comes before {cth_throne} in audience: Yeoul, goddess of the river Sanga, which waters one poor world and nothing else. She is muddy to the knees and very plain-spoken. A great lord upstream wants to dam her river for a lake in front of his new palace. The court laughs at her boots. Her ferryman, an old ghost called Doksuri, holds her hat.

choices.text: Rule for Yeoul

effects.log: You rule for her before she has finished. The great lord is offended. Yeoul is not grateful, exactly; she says it was obviously right. You find yourself agreeing, and smiling.

choices.text: Ask to see the river before you rule

effects.log: Yeoul looks at you for the first time as if you might be worth the climb. "Bring boots," she says.

choices.text: Rule for the great lord, with a payment to her

effects.log: The lord gets his lake. Yeoul takes the payment, puts it in Doksuri's hat, and walks out. The court stops laughing, briefly.

events.text: You go down to the river Sanga in borrowed boots. Doksuri rows you, slowly, telling you the name of every bend. Yeoul shows you the world it waters: rice terraces, a mill, children fishing with string. It is the most peaceful season you have spent since you took the throne.

choices.text: Stay the whole season

effects.log: You stay. The court sends seven increasingly urgent messages. You answer them from the riverbank. Doksuri teaches you to row badly.

choices.text: Offer Yeoul a post at court

effects.log: "And who would keep the river?" she says. She does not say no. She does not say yes. Doksuri, behind her, looks very worried.

events.text: Word has got about. {cth_Court} knows you mean to take Yeoul as consort. The council objects, all of it, in order: a small god, a muddy river, no house, no army, no library. A great house offers you instead its finest daughter, with three domains. Yeoul has heard too, and has sent no word at all.

choices.text: Take Yeoul as consort

effects.log: You announce it before the council has finished objecting. Yeoul arrives at court in clean boots, which is how you know she is frightened. Doksuri rows her up the last stair.

choices.text: Let it go, and keep her as a friend

effects.log: You send Yeoul a letter, the hardest you have written. Her answer comes by river, a single line: "Of course. Mind your boots." The council is relieved. You are not.

events.text: Yeoul is unhappy at court. She is polite and plain and the court cannot bear her, and she cannot bear the court. Downriver, the Sanga runs low without her. Doksuri comes to you, cap in hand, and asks if she might go home half of every year, to keep the river.

choices.text: Let her go home half of every year

effects.log: She goes every spring and comes back every autumn, muddy. The Sanga runs full. The court makes jokes about it. You take to visiting in spring.

choices.text: Ask her to stay, and send a lesser god to keep the river

effects.log: She stays. The lesser god is careless, and the Sanga silts. Yeoul says nothing, but she stands at the window every morning looking down.

events.text: The great lord upstream has not forgotten. In a dry age he dams the Sanga after all, quietly, to fill his palace lake, and tells the council the consort's river was always a ditch. Yeoul comes to you dry-eyed and furious, with a jar of silt from the riverbed.

choices.text: Break the dam yourself

effects.log: You go down and break it with one hand. The Sanga runs. The lord's lake becomes a pleasant meadow. The court is shocked, and then remembers who sits {cth_throne}.

choices.text: Take him to the judges

effects.log: The judges take twelve years. The Sanga is dry for twelve years. The dam comes down. Yeoul forgives the judges, eventually, and you, a little sooner.

effects.log: You rule for the Sanga before he has wrung out his cap. He rows home the same day. A month later a single fish arrives at your court, wrapped in a leaf, with no letter.

choices.text: Go down and see her

effects.log: You go down in old boots. Yeoul is standing in the riverbed with her sleeves rolled up. She does not ask. You stand in it beside her until the lord gives up.

events.text: A small shrine has gone up on the river Sanga, below the mill. It is to you: the children who fish with string were told a god came down once and rode in Doksuri's boat, rowing badly. Yeoul sends you word that the river is full, and the children are sorry, but they made the god's oar crooked.

choices.text: Send the children a straight oar

effects.log: They put it in the shrine beside the crooked one. Doksuri says the crooked one is more popular.

choices.text: Go down and row again, badly

effects.log: You row Doksuri's boat the length of the Sanga while Yeoul laughs from the bank. It is the best day of your reign, and nobody at court will ever know.

events.text: The war with {cth_foe} has run long, and you decide to send a herald. You choose Gaeul: young, a goddess of the first cold morning of autumn, so eager she has already packed. Everyone else says send someone older. Gaeul says older heralds have been sent for an age, and look.

choices.text: Give her sealed terms of peace

effects.log: You seal the terms with your own seal. Gaeul holds them as though they were hot. She goes before dawn, and the first morning of autumn comes early everywhere she passes.

choices.text: Give her only words, to speak aloud

effects.log: No paper that can be read by the wrong eyes. You make her learn them by heart. She recites them perfectly, then once more, then goes.

events.text: A letter from Gaeul, ten years on. The hostile throne's chamberlain, a heavy smooth god called Ogwang, has kept her from the audience hall for a decade with one courtesy after another. She has found out why. Ogwang sells the war's prayers to both sides. Peace would ruin him.

choices.text: Tell her to be patient and polite

effects.log: She is patient and polite for another five years. She writes that she has learned the name of every one of Ogwang's servants, and that some of them dislike him.

choices.text: Tell her how to go round him

ok.log: You know the old doors of that court from the last war. Gaeul goes round by the kitchens and reaches the throne in a month. Ogwang finds out a month after that.

fail.log: Your doors have been bricked up since the last war. Gaeul is caught in a corridor, and Ogwang is now very attentive to her.

choices.text: Send Ogwang a gift

effects.log: You send him a very great gift. He accepts it, and Gaeul is seen within the year. You have paid the man who profits from the war. You do not like the taste of it.

events.text: Gaeul has reached the hostile throne. Its ruler is old and tired and wants peace, and does not trust you an inch. The answer comes in Gaeul's hand: they will talk, if you come yourself, through the middle of their Host, or if Gaeul stays among them as a pledge for as long as the talking lasts.

choices.text: Go yourself

effects.log: You go, against the advice of every god in {cth_court}. The road runs between two armies who have not seen each other's faces in an age, and both are watching you.

choices.text: Let Gaeul stay as the pledge

effects.log: Gaeul writes back at once: yes. She is proud and she is frightened, and she says both in the same line. The talking begins.

effects.log: You send him a very great gift. He accepts it, and Gaeul is seen within the year. You have paid the man who profits from the war. You do not like the taste of it.

events.text: Gaeul has reached the hostile throne. Its ruler is old and tired and wants peace, and does not trust you an inch. The answer comes in Gaeul's hand: they will talk, if you come yourself, through the middle of their Host, or if Gaeul stays among them as a pledge for as long as the talking lasts.

choices.text: Go yourself

effects.log: You go, against the advice of every god in {cth_court}. The road runs between two armies who have not seen each other's faces in an age, and both are watching you.

choices.text: Let Gaeul stay as the pledge

effects.log: Gaeul writes back at once: yes. She is proud and she is frightened, and she says both in the same line. The talking begins.

events.text: In the hall of {cth_foe}, Ogwang meets you at the door, all smoothness, and shows you to a seat placed just below the throne, so that the whole court can see you sit lower. Gaeul, at your shoulder, has gone very still. The old ruler of {cth_foe} watches to see what you will do.

choices.text: Stand, and stay standing

effects.log: You stand through the whole first day. On the second, the old ruler stands too, and the chair is quietly taken away. Ogwang is not at the door on the third.

choices.text: Sit, and talk as if it were the highest seat in heaven

effects.log: You sit and talk well. By evening nobody remembers where you sat, only what you said. Ogwang, defeated by your manners, goes home early.

events.text: The peace is written: not a good one, but a real one, with a border down the middle of a sky. On the road home Gaeul is quiet for a week, then says she thinks she will not be a herald any more. She would like a small domain of her own: one cold morning, somewhere nobody fights.

choices.text: Give her the first cold morning of a quiet world

effects.log: You give it to her in writing, with your seal. Every autumn, after, that world has a perfect first cold morning. Its people say it smells of peace and woodsmoke.

choices.text: Ask her to stay on, as your first herald

effects.log: She stays, for you. She is the best herald in heaven for an age. Every autumn she goes, for one morning, somewhere nobody fights.

events.text: Gaeul has been a pledge at the court of {cth_foe} for six years while the talking goes on. Her letters are long and funny and getting thinner. In the last one she says Ogwang has offered her a seat on his own council, and an end to the waiting, if she will tell him your terms before you send them.

choices.text: Send her the terms yourself, all of them

effects.log: You send her everything. She hands it to the old ruler, not to Ogwang. The old ruler laughs for the first time in an age, and Ogwang is sent to count fish.

choices.text: Tell her to refuse, and wait

effects.log: She refuses. Ogwang makes her life very small for a year. She writes you a letter entirely about the weather, which is how you know.

events.text: The peace is signed, and Gaeul comes home after nine years. She has grown older in the eyes, the way gods do only from waiting. She brings a letter from the old ruler of {cth_foe}, addressed to you in a shaky hand: Your herald was the best of your terms.

choices.text: Read the letter to the whole court

effects.log: You read it aloud, and Gaeul goes the colour of an autumn leaf. Nobody in {cth_court} says send someone older again.

choices.text: Give the letter to Gaeul to keep

effects.log: You give it to her. She keeps it on her wall in a plain frame, beside a map of every corridor in the court of {cth_foe}.
